citation.title: Deep reinforcement learning for engineering design through topology optimization of elementally discretized design domains
citation.authors: Nathan K. Brown, Anthony P. Garland, Georges M. Fadel, Gang Li

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: The RL agent produces compliance-minimizing topologies with performance similar to or better than gradient-based topology optimization.
claim.key_phrase: similar or better compliance minimization performance
claim.alternatives: Section 4.2/Table 1 gives quantitative strain-energy and volume-fraction comparisons for RL and 99-line SIMP designs; the paper reports lower strain energy for RL in all but load case D.

baseline.implementation: Sigmund's 99-line SIMP algorithm; penalty factor 3 and filter radius 1.5
baseline.hardware_ml: PC with Intel Core i7-10510U CPU at 1.80 GHz and 16 GB RAM (training; Section 4.1); test hardware not separately specified
baseline.problem_size: 2D, final 24x24 topology; RL trained at 6x6 and progressively refined through 12x12
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated; training uses online episodic interactions and FEA (Sections 3.2, 4.1)
baseline.quality_metric: final strain energy (cF) and final volume fraction (VFF); allowable stress increase or target volume fraction (Table 1)
baseline.quality_gap: Table 1 reports lower strain energy for RL than the gradient-based design in all load cases except D; exact values vary by case.

R1.evidence: Abstract: primary comparison concerns design quality and makes no speed comparison.

R2.evidence: Sections 3–4: no qualifying classical solver, hardware mismatch, iteration-count, or per-iteration-time issue is established.

R3.evidence: Abstract: primary outcome is quality-only; no speed claim requires amortized cost accounting.

R4.evidence: Sections 3–4/Table 1: returned designs are assessed with FEA-based strain energy and volume fraction; Section 5.2 discusses sub-optimal outputs, but failure/infeasibility rates are not reported.

notes: Open-access version of record read from the author-hosted PDF. The article links to public code/data, but its text does not state a reuse license, so retest eligibility is not established.
